title: The ULTIMATE Forearm Exercises Tier-List (Popeye-tier to Skeletor-tier)
summary: NH ranks about 50 forearm exercises, tools and sports from Skeletor (D) to Popeye (S) tier, judging each by whether it targets a forearm function (wrist flexion/extension, pronation/supination, elbow flexion, isometric grip) without taxing the rest of the body. His top picks are the dead hang, supinated forearm curl, preacher hammer curl, pronation twist, standing thumbless reverse curl, wrist roller done T-rex style, dumbbell finger curls and the rope hangman curl; compounds like deadlifts and rows train forearms only as a byproduct.
claims: The forearms are one of the most underrated muscle groups: many people never train them, and those who do mostly spam bad movements
Judge a forearm exercise by which forearm function it trains (wrist flexion/extension, pronation/supination, elbow flexion, isometric hold) and how well it does it
You do not need to know detailed forearm anatomy to grow them; many people with huge forearms couldn't locate their pronator
The number one mistake is using movements that train the forearm only as a byproduct; to get big forearms you must treat them as a priority
Deadlifting for forearms is the worst advice: letting grip limit a posterior-chain lift gives you neither forearms nor back gains (D tier)
A mixed grip does not train forearms more; it only stops the bar rolling, which straps do better, and the stimulus-to-fatigue ratio for forearms is terrible
Barbell rows are an upper-back lift and a mediocre (C tier) forearm exercise; dumbbell rows sit between C and B
Pull-ups are a decent (B tier) forearm exercise, better than rows and deadlifts; if your hands open before your back fails you have a grip-to-back strength imbalance to fix
Rack pulls from above the knee, without straps and with a normal double-overhand grip, are an A tier forearm exercise because the bar never rolls and the lower back is barely taxed
Farmer's walks without straps for time will grow your forearms (A tier), but they tax the rest of the body too much to be S tier; strongmen have jacked forearms from them
Frequency is the number one factor for growing forearms, which requires exercises that target only them, since compounds fatigue the whole body
The dead hang is S tier: it isolates the forearm grip, decompresses the spine and aids recovery; do one at the end of every lower body day
Building dead hangs up to 2-4 minutes will bring visible forearm development
Behind-the-back wrist curls allow heavy loads but have a poor, unnatural range of motion and clash with big glutes; C tier
Regular wrist curls, especially pronated, are B tier: many people never feel them in the muscle and they gave him wrist tendinitis no matter his form
The goal of forearm training is to train the muscle, not the tendon
Gooseneck wrist curls, an old-school variation, are better for hypertrophy than normal wrist curls; uncomfortable but A tier
A supinated forearm curl with an appropriate, non-overextended range of motion is the king of wrist curls and S tier for the inner forearm
Regular biceps curls train the inner forearm as a byproduct (many people have dominant inner forearms from spamming curls) but are only C tier for forearms
Pinwheel (cross-body) curls are his favourite curl and B tier for forearms; hammer curls are A tier as a brachioradialis builder even though they hurt his shoulders
The preacher station is the best piece of equipment for forearms; preacher hammer curls are S tier because they lock the shoulder and elbow and give a big stretch
Arm wrestlers have the biggest forearms pound for pound of any athlete; arm wrestling as a sport is A tier
Never let the wrist break back on forearm work: keep it stacked and strong, or you risk tendinitis
Arm wrestlers train forearms 5-6 times a day without burning out, showing that work capacity must be built before forearms grow
Rock climbing builds back and forearms (B tier) but is limited to bodyweight loading
The pronation twist, learned from arm wrestlers, is S tier: load the hand with a belt or loop and rotate inward; it is joint-friendly and grows the often-neglected pronator
A well-developed pronator bulges visibly and is often mistaken for a tendon; arm wrestlers, climbers and guitarists have big ones
Supination work is only B tier for gym rats because curls already train supination
Dumbbell wrist twists are D tier: the weight pulls sideways instead of down, cannot be loaded properly and leads to tendinitis; train rotation with a belt loop and plates instead
Reverse curls are S tier when done standing but only C tier on the preacher, where the bar drifts away from the stacked wrist and onto the fingertips
Use a thumbless grip on reverse curls so the bar sits in a pocket and cannot creep; thumbless grip as a technique is B tier and also worth trying on pull-ups
Wrapping a towel around any implement upgrades it for forearms (towel rows go from C to B); use a thick, rough, non-absorbent towel
Fat grips are A tier and turn mediocre movements into good forearm exercises; avoid overpriced ones and pick a size where your fingers can barely touch
Axle bars are good but only B tier because their thickness is fixed, unlike adaptable fat grips
Plate pinches are C tier because they are impractical to progressively overload
Plate flips are a D tier circus act that trains coordination more than grip and risks broken toes
Kettlebell flips are B tier: the bell is made to be grabbed and the move stresses only the forearms
The hallmark of a good forearm exercise is that it stimulates only the forearms without taxing other joints or muscles
The back works in the bottom and middle of a pull-up; top-range partial neutral-grip pull-ups (arm wrestling pull-ups) mostly train forearms and are A tier
The newspaper twist gives a burn but no mass and cannot be progressed; D tier
Finger extensions with an elastic band are good for blood flow and elbow or wrist pain but not hypertrophy; they gave him knuckle tendinitis
Opening and closing the hand in a rice bucket is B tier active recovery that gives a big pump
Grip-sport tools work (A tier) but cost 50-60 dollars; there are cheaper ways
The wrist roller is S tier and a must for home gyms, but do it T-rex style with elbows bent, not arms extended, so the shoulders don't limit the set
Hand grippers are C tier: concentric-only crush with no negative; strongmen, climbers and arm wrestlers don't use them
After 11-12 years of grippers (up to Captain of Crush 2.5) his forearms grew from reverse curls, wrist curls and arm wrestling pull-ups, not grippers
Finger curls are the superior replacement for grippers: letting the weight roll to the fingertips gives a loaded negative; cable version A tier, dumbbell version S tier
Anyone doing wrist curls should switch to finger curls for 1-2 weeks and will never go back
Finger curl machines are C tier: free weights outdo them and isolation should be done light
Plastic 'forearm developer' gadgets are D tier marketing products that limit range of motion and progression
Rings are C tier for forearms (thumbless rows), still better value than single-purpose gadgets
Resisting a hammer's leverage is a B tier grip-sport test but hard to progress
Spring-based forearm twisters are inferior to the wrist roller: less stretch, discomfort, wrist problems and high price
Knuckle push-ups, fingertip push-ups and fingertip pull-ups do nothing for forearm hypertrophy beyond finger resilience
Rope climbing or rope pulling is B tier: full-hand grip with control of wrist and elbow angle
The hangman curl (neutral-grip rope curl on a cable or a rope looped through a plate) is S tier: constant tension, stretched negative and free wrist angle
Zottman curls are C tier: a lift that trains more than forearms trains forearms poorly, and the forearms limit the biceps load
Naturals with the biggest forearms are usually older lifters because forearms take years; expect 1-3 years from stick to big forearms
